content: Infantile colic is characterized by intense crying episodes lasting at least three hours per day, occurring on at least three days per week, for a minimum of three weeks. It is most commonly observed during the first six weeks of life, with a prevalence ranging from 17% to 25%, depending on the population and definitions used. The condition typically resolves by three months of age. The exact cause of infantile colic remains unclear, but it is believed to be multifactorial, involving psychological, behavioral, and biological factors such as food hypersensitivity, allergies, gut microbiota imbalances, and gastrointestinal dysmotility. The role of dietary changes in managing colic is debated. A systematic review was conducted to evaluate the effects of dietary modifications on reducing colic in infants younger than four months. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-RCTs that assessed dietary interventions, either alone or in combination, compared to other treatments or placebos. The primary outcome was the duration of crying, while secondary outcomes included response to intervention, frequency of crying episodes, parental and family quality of life, infant sleep duration, parental satisfaction, and adverse effects. Fifteen RCTs involving 1121 infants aged 2 to 16 weeks were included in the review. The studies were small and had a high risk of bias due to various design flaws. The interventions varied widely, precluding meta-analysis. The quality of evidence was rated as very low using the GRADE system. None of the studies reported on parental or family quality of life, infant sleep duration, or parental satisfaction. 1. Low-Allergen Maternal Diet vs. Maternal Diet with Potential Allergens: One study involving 90 infants found that 74% of infants (35/47) responded to a low-allergen maternal diet, defined as a reduction in crying or fussing duration by 25%, compared to 37% (16/43) of infants whose mothers consumed a diet containing potential allergens. The difference was statistically significant (37% difference; 95% CI 18 to 56; P < 0.001). 2. Low-Allergen Diet or Soy Milk Formula vs. Standard Diet or Cow's Milk Formula with Dicyclomine Hydrochloride: In a study of 120 infants, 66.6% (10/15) of breastfed infants responded to dicyclomine hydrochloride with a normal diet, compared to 62.5% (10/16) on a low-allergen diet. Among formula-fed infants, 53.3% (24/45) taking dicyclomine hydrochloride improved, compared to 65.9% (29/44) on soy milk formula. Response was defined as crying less than one hour per day after 48 hours of treatment, with remission lasting one month. 3. Hydrolyzed Formula vs. Standard Formula: One study of 43 infants reported that 8/23 infants in the whey hydrolysate group responded to the intervention (crying less than three hours per day on at least three days per week), compared to 5/20 in the standard formula group (P = 0.65). However, the same study found a greater reduction in crying time with hydrolyzed formula (104 minutes/day, 95% CI 55 to 155) compared to standard formula (3 minutes/day, 95% CI −63 to 67), with a significant difference of 101 minutes/day (95% CI 25 to 179; P = 0.02). No adverse effects were reported. 4. Hydrolyzed Formula or Dairyand Soy-Free Maternal Diet vs. Standard Diet/Formula with Parental Education or Counseling: A study of 21 infants found that crying time decreased to 2.03 hours/day (SD 1.03) in the hydrolyzed formula or dairyand soy-free maternal diet group, compared to 1.08 hours/day (SD 0.7) in the parental education or counseling group, nine days post-intervention. 5. Partially Hydrolyzed, Lower Lactose, Whey-Based Formula with Oligosaccharides vs. Standard Formula with Simethicone: A study of 267 infants found that both groups experienced a reduction in colic episodes after seven days. The partially hydrolyzed formula group showed a decrease from 5.99 episodes/day (SD 1.84) to 2.47 episodes/day (SD 1.94), while the standard formula group decreased from 5.41 episodes/day (SD 1.88) to 3.72 episodes/day (SD 1.98). The difference was statistically significant (P < 0.001). After two weeks, the partially hydrolyzed formula group had 1.76 episodes/day (SD 1.60) compared to 3.32 episodes/day (SD 2.06) in the standard formula group (P < 0.001). No adverse effects were reported. 6. Lactase Enzyme Supplementation vs. Placebo: Three studies involving 138 infants assessed this intervention, but as they were cross-over trials, pre-washout data were not reported. No adverse effects were noted. 7. Herbal Extract (Foeniculum vulgare, Matricaria recutita, and Melissa officinalis) vs. Placebo: One study of 93 infants found that the average daily crying time was significantly lower in the herbal extract group (76.9 minutes/day, SD 23.5) compared to the placebo group (169.9 minutes/day, SD 23.1) at the end of the one-week study (95% CI −102.89 to −83.11; P < 0.01). No adverse effects were reported. 8. Soy Protein-Based Formula vs. Standard Cow's Milk Protein-Based Formula: One study of 19 infants reported a mean crying time of 12.7 hours/week (SD 16.4) in the soy formula group compared to 17.3 hours/week (SD 6.9) in the standard cow's milk formula group. Additionally, 50% (5/10) of infants in the soy formula group responded, compared to 0% (0/9) in the standard cow's milk group. 9. Soy Protein Formula with Polysaccharide vs. Standard Soy Protein Formula: One cross-over study of 27 infants assessed this comparison but did not provide pre-washout data. In conclusion, the evidence supporting dietary modifications for the treatment of infantile colic is limited and of very low quality. The studies included in this review were small, had significant methodological limitations, and produced inconsistent results. There is insufficient evidence to recommend any specific dietary intervention for colic. Further research with robust study designs, larger sample sizes, and clinically meaningful outcomes is needed.
